title: When would you use WebSockets vs polling vs SSE?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** needs to understand `realtime` to make architecture decisions
* **User** evaluates trade-offs for when would you use websockets vs polling vs sse under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to realtime
* **Service** implements When would you use WebSockets vs polling vs SSE with configurable policy
* **Service** exposes metrics and handles failure modes gracefully

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Client -> Web Server -> API -> Cache/DB (When would you use WebSockets vs...)</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Client + LB</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">DNS / CDN</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">L4/L7 LB</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">health checks</text><path class="d-edge" d="M 260 85 L 300 85" marker-end="url(#a)"/><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">API + Cache</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">stateless API</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">Redis / Memcached</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">write-through</text><path class="d-edge" d="M 520 85 L 560 85" marker-end="url(#a)"/><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">DB + Store</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">SQL/NoSQL</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">object store S3</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">WAL replica</text></svg>

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For when would you use websockets vs polling vs sse? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo
def hash_key(k): return int(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest(),16)

class Bucket:
  def __init__(self, cap, refill):
    self.cap=cap; self.tokens=cap; self.refill=refill; self.last=time.time()
  def allow(self,n=1):
    now=time.time(); self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.last)*self.refill)
    self.last=now
    if self.tokens>=n:
      self.tokens-=n; return True
    return False

b=Bucket(100,10)
print(b.allow())
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `python`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

## Step 4: Scale the design

> Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

**Important: Do not simply jump to the final design. State you would do this iteratively: 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks, 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating trade-offs, and 4) repeat. See [Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#design-a-system-that-scales-to-millions-of-users-on-aws) as sample.**

<svg class="iq-diagram" viewBox="0 0 820 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11">Scaled: DNS -> CDN -> LB -> Cache -> Sharded DB + Queue</text><rect x="40" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box"/><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22c55e">Edge + LB</text><text x="150" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">DNS anycast</text><text x="150" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">CDN cache</text><text x="150" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">L4/L7 LB</text><path class="d-edge" d="M 260 85 L 300 85" marker-end="url(#a)"/><rect x="300" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box"/><text x="410" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#f59e0b">App + Cache</text><text x="410" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">stateless API</text><text x="410" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">Redis cluster</text><text x="410" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">local cache</text><path class="d-edge" d="M 520 85 L 560 85" marker-end="url(#a)"/><rect x="560" y="40" width="220" height="90" rx="14" class="d-box"/><text x="670" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#3b82f6">Store + Queue</text><text x="670" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">sharded DB</text><text x="670" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">Kafka / SQS</text><text x="670" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" class="d-sub">replica + WAL</text></svg>

Scales via:

* [DNS](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#domain-name-system) with Route 53 weighted/latency routing + health checks
* [CDN](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#content-delivery-network) (CloudFront/Cloudflare) for static and cacheable dynamic — offloads origin, 95%+ hit rate with tiered cache
* [Load balancer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#load-balancer) L4 (NLB) + L7 (ALB) with least-connections/IP-hash, health checks remove unhealthy nodes
* [Horizontal scaling](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#horizontal-scaling) of stateless API/Web — add nodes behind LB, no sticky sessions
* [Web server (reverse proxy)](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server) caching + TLS
* [API server (application layer)](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#application-layer) with circuit breaker and bulkhead
* [Cache](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#cache) Redis cluster sharded with [consistent hashing](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#consistent-hashing), LRU, TTL, cache-aside vs write-through
* [Relational database](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#relational-database-management-system-rdbms) master-slave replication + [fail-over](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#fail-over), [sharding](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sharding)/[federation](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#federation) when single master limits writes
* [Asynchronism](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#asynchronism) via [message queues](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#message-queues)/task queues for analytics and side-effects, handling [back pressure](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#back-pressure)
* [Consistency patterns](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#consistency-patterns) and [availability patterns](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#availability-patterns) + [CAP](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#cap-theorem)

Quantitative justification: cache hit 90% drops DB QPS 10x (400 QPS -> 40). Sharding by hash(id) spreads writes; N replicas with quorum W+R>N for strong consistency if needed. Queue buffers 5x peak to protect DB. CDN cuts latency from 200ms to 20ms globally. Quantify: P99 200ms, SLO 99.99%, cost per 1M req ~ $X via BoE.

### Additional talking points

> Additional topics to dive into, depending on scope and time.

* **NoSQL**: [Key-value](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#key-value-store), [Document](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#document-store), [Wide column](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#wide-column-store), [Graph](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#graph-database), [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql)
* **Caching**: [Client](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#client-caching), [CDN](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#cdn-caching), [Web server](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#web-server-caching), [Database](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#database-caching), [Application](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#application-caching); [Cache-aside](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#cache-aside), [Write-through](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#write-through), [Write-behind](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#write-behind-write-back), [Refresh-ahead](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#refresh-ahead)
* **Asynchronism**: [Message queues](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#message-queues), [Task queues](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#task-queues), [Back pressure](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#back-pressure), [Microservices](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#microservices)
* **Communications**: [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest) vs [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), [Service discovery](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#service-discovery)
* **Security**: [Security](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#security) — auth, TLS, rate limiting, input validation
* **Latency numbers**: [Latency numbers every programmer should know](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know)
* **Interview tip**: Drive the discussion, quantify trade-offs, and iterate — do not jump to final design. Mention [Interview tips](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#how-to-approach-the-system-design-interview-questions) and [Anki flashcards](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#anki-flashcards) for prep.

title: How would you design a notification system?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** performs core action described in How would you design a notification system?
* **User** reads/views result with low latency (<200ms P99)
* **User** expects durability and availability across AZs
* **Service** processes requests via stateless API + queue
* **Service** stores data durably and serves via cache + DB
* **Service** provides analytics and retention

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Schema (DDL):

```sql

  payload JSON NOT NULL,

  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
```

```bash
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```javascript
// Node consistent hash snippet
function hash(s){ let h=0; for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++) h=(h*31+s.charCodeAt(i))>>>0; return h; }
class Ring{
  constructor(nodes, vnodes=100){
    this.ring=[];
    for(const n of nodes) for(let i=0;i<vnodes;i++){
      this.ring.push({h:hash(n+'#'+i), n});
    }
    this.ring.sort((a,b)=>a.h-b.h);
  }
  get(key){
    const h=hash(key);
    let best=this.ring.find(x=>x.h>=h) || this.ring[0];
    return best.n;
  }
}
console.log(new Ring(['a','b','c']).get('user:123'));
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `javascript`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

> Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

**Important: Do not simply jump to the final design. title: What is the circuit breaker pattern?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** needs to understand `circuit-breaker` to make architecture decisions
* **User** evaluates trade-offs for the circuit breaker pattern under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to circuit-breaker
* **Service** implements What is the circuit breaker pattern with configurable policy
* **Service** exposes metrics and handles failure modes gracefully

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For what is the circuit breaker pattern? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```java
public class Algo {
  public static String base62(long n){
    String a="0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
    StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();
    while(n>0){ s.append(a.charAt((int)(n%62))); n/=62; }
    return s.reverse().toString();
  }
  public static void main(String[] args){
    System.out.println(base62(123456789L));
  }
}
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `java`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

State you would do this iteratively: 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks, 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating trade-offs, and 4) repeat. // Node consistent hash snippet
```javascript
function hash(s){ let h=0; for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++) h=(h*31+s.charCodeAt(i))>>>0; return h; }

  constructor(nodes, vnodes=100){
    this.ring=[];
    for(const n of nodes) for(let i=0;i<vnodes;i++){
      this.ring.push({h:hash(n+'#'+i), n});
    }
    this.ring.sort((a,b)=>a.h-b.h);
  }
  get(key){
    const h=hash(key);
    let best=this.ring.find(x=>x.h>=h) || this.ring[0];
    return best.n;
  }
}
```

answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

### Use case: primary flow

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```java
public class Algo {
  public static String base62(long n){
    String a="0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
    StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();
    while(n>0){ s.append(a.charAt((int)(n%62))); n/=62; }
    return s.reverse().toString();
  }
  public static void main(String[] args){
    System.out.println(base62(123456789L));
  }
}
```

* [Horizontal scaling](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#horizontal-scaling) of stateless API/Web — add nodes behind LB, no sticky sessions
* [Web server (reverse proxy)](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server) caching + TLS
* [API server (application layer)](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#application-layer) with circuit breaker and bulkhead
* [Cache](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#cache) Redis cluster sharded with [consistent hashing](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#consistent-hashing), LRU, TTL, cache-aside vs write-through

title: What is leader election in distributed systems?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** needs to understand `leader-election` to make architecture decisions
* **User** evaluates trade-offs for leader election in distributed systems under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to leader-election
* **Service** implements What is leader election in distributed systems with configurable policy
* **Service** exposes metrics and handles failure modes gracefully

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For what is leader election in distributed systems? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo
def hash_key(k): return int(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest(),16)

class Bucket:
  def __init__(self, cap, refill):
    self.cap=cap; self.tokens=cap; self.refill=refill; self.last=time.time()
  def allow(self,n=1):
    now=time.time(); self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.last)*self.refill)
    self.last=now
    if self.tokens>=n:
      self.tokens-=n; return True
    return False

b=Bucket(100,10)
print(b.allow())
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `python`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

```javascript
function hash(s){ let h=0; for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++) h=(h*31+s.charCodeAt(i))>>>0; return h; }
```

answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

* **User** evaluates trade-offs for database connection pooling under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to connection-pool
* **Service** implements What is database connection pooling with configurable policy
* **Service** exposes metrics and handles failure modes gracefully

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |


Algorithm / core logic:

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo
def hash_key(k): return int(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest(),16)

class Bucket:
  def __init__(self, cap, refill):
    self.cap=cap; self.tokens=cap; self.refill=refill; self.last=time.time()
  def allow(self,n=1):
    now=time.time(); self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.last)*self.refill)
    self.last=now
    if self.tokens>=n:
      self.tokens-=n; return True
    return False

b=Bucket(100,10)
print(b.allow())
```

title: How would you design a file storage service like Dropbox?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** performs core action described in How would you design a file storage service like Dropbox?
* **User** reads/views result with low latency (<200ms P99)
* **User** expects durability and availability across AZs
* **Service** processes requests via stateless API + queue
* **Service** stores data durably and serves via cache + DB
* **Service** provides analytics and retention

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For how would you design a file storage service like dropbox? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```javascript
// Node consistent hash snippet
function hash(s){ let h=0; for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++) h=(h*31+s.charCodeAt(i))>>>0; return h; }
class Ring{
  constructor(nodes, vnodes=100){
    this.ring=[];
    for(const n of nodes) for(let i=0;i<vnodes;i++){
      this.ring.push({h:hash(n+'#'+i), n});
    }
    this.ring.sort((a,b)=>a.h-b.h);
  }
  get(key){
    const h=hash(key);
    let best=this.ring.find(x=>x.h>=h) || this.ring[0];
    return best.n;
  }
}
console.log(new Ring(['a','b','c']).get('user:123'));
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `javascript`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

## Step 4: Scale the design

> Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

**Important: Do not simply jump to the final design. State you would do this iteratively: 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks, 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating trade-offs, and 4) repeat. See [Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#design-a-system-that-scales-to-millions-of-users-on-aws) as sample.**

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo

class Bucket:
  def __init__(self, cap, refill):
    self.cap=cap; self.tokens=cap; self.refill=refill; self.last=time.time()
  def allow(self,n=1):
    now=time.time(); self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.last)*self.refill)
```

## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** performs core action described in How would you design a 'nearby drivers' / proximity search?
* **User** reads/views result with low latency (<200ms P99)

title: How would you design a distributed cache?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** performs core action described in How would you design a distributed cache?
* **User** reads/views result with low latency (<200ms P99)
* **User** expects durability and availability across AZs
* **Service** processes requests via stateless API + queue
* **Service** stores data durably and serves via cache + DB
* **Service** provides analytics and retention

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

For how would you design a distributed cache? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
-- Cache is Redis/Memcached, not SQL; table shown for fallback DB
CREATE TABLE cache_fallback (
  k VARCHAR(256) PRIMARY KEY,
  v BLOB NOT NULL,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl https://api.example.com/v1/items/123
# X-Cache: HIT (age 12s) or MISS
# Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```javascript
class LRU{
  constructor(cap){this.cap=cap; this.m=new Map();}
  get(k){ if(!this.m.has(k)) return -1; const v=this.m.get(k); this.m.delete(k); this.m.set(k,v); return v; }
  put(k,v){ if(this.m.has(k)) this.m.delete(k); this.m.set(k,v); if(this.m.size>this.cap) this.m.delete(this.m.keys().next().value); }
}
const l=new LRU(2); l.put(1,1); console.log(l.get(1));
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `javascript`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo
```

title: Why prefer stateless services and how do you handle sessions?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** needs to understand `stateless` to make architecture decisions
* **User** evaluates trade-offs for why prefer stateless services and how do you handle sessions under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to stateless
* **Service** implements Why prefer stateless services and how do you handle sessions with configurable policy
* **Service** exposes metrics and handles failure modes gracefully

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For why prefer stateless services and how do you handle sessions? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```java
public class Algo {
  public static String base62(long n){
    String a="0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
    StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();
    while(n>0){ s.append(a.charAt((int)(n%62))); n/=62; }
    return s.reverse().toString();
  }
  public static void main(String[] args){
    System.out.println(base62(123456789L));
  }
}
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `java`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

## Step 4: Scale the design

> Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

**Important: Do not simply jump to the final design. State you would do this iteratively: 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks, 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating trade-offs, and 4) repeat. See [Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#design-a-system-that-scales-to-millions-of-users-on-aws) as sample.**

```javascript
// Node consistent hash snippet
function hash(s){ let h=0; for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++) h=(h*31+s.charCodeAt(i))>>>0; return h; }

  constructor(nodes, vnodes=100){
    this.ring=[];
    for(const n of nodes) for(let i=0;i<vnodes;i++){
      this.ring.push({h:hash(n+'#'+i), n});
    }
    this.ring.sort((a,b)=>a.h-b.h);
  }
  get(key){
    const h=hash(key);
    let best=this.ring.find(x=>x.h>=h) || this.ring[0];
    return best.n;
  }
}
```

## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** needs to understand `observability` to make architecture decisions
* **User** evaluates trade-offs for what are the three pillars of observability under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to observability

* Billing/payments detail

```java
public class Algo {
  public static String base62(long n){

    StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();
    while(n>0){ s.append(a.charAt((int)(n%62))); n/=62; }
    return s.reverse().toString();
  }

  }
}
```

title: How would you design an analytics/metrics pipeline?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** performs core action described in How would you design an analytics/metrics pipeline?
* **User** reads/views result with low latency (<200ms P99)
* **User** expects durability and availability across AZs
* **Service** processes requests via stateless API + queue
* **Service** stores data durably and serves via cache + DB
* **Service** provides analytics and retention

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For how would you design an analytics/metrics pipeline? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo
def hash_key(k): return int(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest(),16)

class Bucket:
  def __init__(self, cap, refill):
    self.cap=cap; self.tokens=cap; self.refill=refill; self.last=time.time()
  def allow(self,n=1):
    now=time.time(); self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.last)*self.refill)
    self.last=now
    if self.tokens>=n:
      self.tokens-=n; return True
    return False

b=Bucket(100,10)
print(b.allow())
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `python`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.

## Step 4: Scale the design

> Identify and address bottlenecks, given the constraints.

**Important: Do not simply jump to the final design. State you would do this iteratively: 1) Benchmark/Load Test, 2) Profile for bottlenecks, 3) address bottlenecks while evaluating trade-offs, and 4) repeat. See [Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#design-a-system-that-scales-to-millions-of-users-on-aws) as sample.**

## Step 3: Design core components

### Use case: primary flow

```sql
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash

  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```java
public class Algo {
  public static String base62(long n){
    String a="0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
    StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();
    while(n>0){ s.append(a.charAt((int)(n%62))); n/=62; }
    return s.reverse().toString();
  }
  public static void main(String[] args){
    System.out.println(base62(123456789L));
  }
}
```

title: When do you use a read replica vs a cache?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** needs to understand `read-replica` to make architecture decisions
* **User** evaluates trade-offs for when do you use a read replica vs a cache under load
* **User** debugs production issue related to read-replica
* **Service** implements When do you use a read replica vs a cache with configurable policy
* **Service** exposes metrics and handles failure modes gracefully

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

```javascript
class LRU{
```

title: How do you make a payment system reliable against retries?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** triggers How do you make a payment system reliable against retries? flow via API or client
* **User** expects correctness under concurrency and failures
* **Service** handles scale, availability, and consistency
* **Service** monitors and auto-recovers

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

## Step 3: Design core components

Schema (DDL):


Algorithm / core logic:

```python
import hashlib, bisect, time

# Consistent hash or token bucket generic algo
def hash_key(k): return int(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest(),16)

class Bucket:
  def __init__(self, cap, refill):
    self.cap=cap; self.tokens=cap; self.refill=refill; self.last=time.time()
  def allow(self,n=1):
    now=time.time(); self.tokens=min(self.cap, self.tokens+(now-self.last)*self.refill)
    self.last=now
    if self.tokens>=n:
      self.tokens-=n; return True
    return False

b=Bucket(100,10)
print(b.allow())
```

title: What indexing strategies improve database performance?
answer:
## Step 1: Outline use cases and constraints

> Gather requirements and scope the problem. Ask questions to clarify use cases and constraints. Discuss assumptions.

### Use cases

#### We'll scope the problem to handle only the following use cases

* **User** triggers What indexing strategies improve database performance? flow via API or client
* **User** expects correctness under concurrency and failures
* **Service** handles scale, availability, and consistency
* **Service** monitors and auto-recovers

#### Out of scope

* Advanced ML ranking
* Billing/payments detail
* Full admin console

### Constraints and assumptions

#### State assumptions

* Traffic not evenly distributed (Pareto 80/20)
* High availability 99.99% (52m downtime/yr), durability 99.999999%
* Estimate 10M DAU, 100M requests/day
* Read-heavy or write-heavy per use case, 5x peak over average

#### Calculate usage

**Clarify with your interviewer if you should run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations.**

| field | bytes | note |
| id | 8 bytes | snowflake |
| payload | ~1KB | avg |
| metadata | 50 bytes | timestamps |
* Assume 100M requests/day = 1.16K QPS avg, 5.8K peak; 1KB avg => 100 GB/day ingress, 3 TB/mo with replication; QPS per shard ~1K, so 6 shards.
* Handy conversion guide: 2.5M seconds / month, 1 QPS = 2.5M req/mo, 40 QPS = 100M req/mo, 400 QPS = 1B req/mo. Memory: 1 MB sequential read 250µs, SSD 4x, Disk 80x.

## Step 2: Create a high level design

> Outline a high level design with all important components.

We keep the initial design simple: stateless API behind a load balancer, cache for hot data, and durable storage. This handles the scope in Step 1 while leaving room to scale iteratively.

Client -> Web Server (reverse proxy) -> API -> Cache / DB. The **Web Server** terminates TLS and serves edge cache, the **API** is stateless and horizontally scalable, **Cache** (Redis/Memcached) offloads reads, and the **SQL/NoSQL** + **Object Store** provide durability. For what indexing strategies improve database performance? we choose the store by access pattern described in Step 3.

## Step 3: Design core components

> Dive into details for each core component.

### Use case: primary flow

* The **Client** sends request to the **Web Server**, running as a [reverse proxy](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#reverse-proxy-web-server)
* The **Web Server** forwards to the **Write/Read API** server
* The **API** does: auth, validation, then **Cache** lookup else **SQL Database** / **Object Store** access, then returns response. Internal RPC is via [RPC](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#remote-procedure-call-rpc), external via [REST](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#representational-state-transfer-rest).

**Data store trade-off:** Discuss [SQL vs NoSQL](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#sql-or-nosql). Relational gives ACID and joins; NoSQL (key-value/document) gives flexible schema and high write scale. We pick based on read/write ratio and consistency needs — often both: SQL for metadata, NoSQL/cache for hot path.

Schema (DDL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  payload JSON NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  INDEX(owner_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY HASH(id) PARTITIONS 16;
```

API (REST):

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/entities \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123" \
  -d '{"payload":"hello"}'
# 201 {"id":"123","status":"created"}

curl https://api.example.com/v1/entities/123
# 200 {"id":"123","payload":"hello"}
```

Algorithm / core logic:

```javascript
// Node consistent hash snippet
function hash(s){ let h=0; for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++) h=(h*31+s.charCodeAt(i))>>>0; return h; }
class Ring{
  constructor(nodes, vnodes=100){
    this.ring=[];
    for(const n of nodes) for(let i=0;i<vnodes;i++){
      this.ring.push({h:hash(n+'#'+i), n});
    }
    this.ring.sort((a,b)=>a.h-b.h);
  }
  get(key){
    const h=hash(key);
    let best=this.ring.find(x=>x.h>=h) || this.ring[0];
    return best.n;
  }
}
console.log(new Ring(['a','b','c']).get('user:123'));
```

Additional per-use-case notes: flow is Client->Web Server->API->DB/Cache as above; generation/lookup algorithm runs in `javascript`; API uses `bash curl` examples; DDL uses `sql`. All components are monitored with [latency numbers](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know) in mind.
